content: 1. The South African patient monitoring system includes a Patient Details Folder that records essential demographic and medical information. This includes the patient’s phone number, sex (male or female), and a detailed history of pregnancies, specifying the year, gestational age, delivery details, sex of the baby, birth weight, and outcomes. 2. Social history and support are documented, including risk factors such as family history of heart disease or hypertension, smoking habits (year started, quantity per day, and year stopped if applicable), family history of diabetes, alcohol consumption (type, quantity per week, and year stopped if applicable), family history of triglycerides/cholesterol issues, physical inactivity, family history of mental illness, history of sexual abuse, and substance abuse. 3. A chronic problem list is maintained, detailing the year or date of diagnosis, associated conditions, and relevant notes. Conditions tracked include hypertension, ischemic heart disease/cardiac failure, diabetes, cerebrovascular accidents/transient ischemic attacks, asthma, peripheral artery disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, retinopathy, epilepsy, chronic renal disease, depression, generalized anxiety disorder, psychosis, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and substance-induced disorders. 4. HIV-related information is meticulously recorded, including prior antiretroviral therapy (ART) details, ART regimens, baseline CD4 counts, transfer-in outcomes, and outcomes of extrapulmonary tuberculosis (EPTB) or drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB). Other chronic conditions are also documented with their diagnosis dates and relevant notes. 5. Past medical history is detailed, including allergies and side effects, which are highlighted in red. Blood group and treatment dates are also recorded. 6. Adult patient stationery includes an ID number, first name, surname, address, date of birth, and next of kin (name and contact information). This section is used to maintain an ongoing summary of the patient’s health, ensuring that any clinician reviewing the file in the future can understand the major features of the patient’s clinical course. 7. Key clinical metrics are tracked, such as viral load and ART regimens for HIV, blood pressure and treatment regimens for hypertension, and HbA1c levels and medications for diabetes. Clinicians are encouraged to insert their own headings as needed. 8. Consolidated guidelines for person-centered HIV patient monitoring and case surveillance are followed. This includes recording dates, times, and clinical metrics such as blood pressure, temperature, heart rate, weight, BMI, and waist circumference. 9. Sexual and reproductive health is monitored, including the use of condoms, STI screenings, PAP smears, and contraceptive methods (e.g., oral contraceptives, IUDs, implants, or injections). Pregnancy-related data such as last menstrual period (LMP), symphysis-fundal height (SFH), gestational age (GA), and ultrasound findings are also documented. 10. Lifestyle factors such as smoking, diet, exercise, and substance use are assessed. Mental health evaluations include mood assessments, danger signs, and psychosocial risks. 11. ART adherence and control are monitored, including peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) and seizure control. Observations and disease tracking include vital signs, anthropometric measurements (weight, height, mid-upper arm circumference), and psychosocial risks. 12. HIV and tuberculosis (TB) statuses are tracked, including ART regimens, CD4 counts, viral loads, and TB screening (IPT, drug-sensitive TB, drug-resistant TB). Barcodes are used for additional coding if necessary. 13. Laboratory investigations include creatinine, eGFR, RPR, Hb, ALT, cholesterol, triglycerides, HbA1c, and urinalysis (including pregnancy tests and glucose levels). 14. Reproductive health assessments include STI screenings, family planning, MMC (medical male circumcision), PAP smears, breast exams, and pregnancy monitoring (LMP, SFH, GA, and ultrasound findings). 15. Appointments, referrals, and discharges are recorded, along with tests conducted and the healthcare provider responsible (nurse, doctor, or data capturer). Management plans, medications, and investigations are documented, including TB diagnostics (e.g., GeneXpert, creatinine, eGFR, RPR). 16. Additional notes include the date of the next visit, the healthcare provider to be seen, and the name and signature of the clinician. Results from investigations such as HbA1c, cholesterol, triglycerides, ECG, X-rays, and other tests are recorded. 17. Adherence to treatment and control of conditions are monitored, including lifestyle factors (smoking, diet, exercise, and substance use) and mental health (mood, substance abuse, and psychosocial risks). 18. Observations and disease tracking include vital signs (blood pressure, temperature, heart rate), anthropometric measurements (weight, height, BMI), and psychosocial risks. 19. HIV and TB statuses are continuously monitored, with ART regimens, CD4 counts, viral loads, and TB screening outcomes documented. Barcodes are used for additional coding if necessary. 20. Laboratory investigations and reproductive health assessments are conducted regularly, ensuring comprehensive patient care and monitoring.
